name: Pliny the Younger
label: Outside witness
knownFor: A Roman governor whose letter to the emperor Trajan tells how he tried Christians in Bithynia and what they told him of their worship.
dates: Governor of Bithynia from 110 or 111; wrote to Trajan probably within a year

keyWorks.title: Letters, Book 10, letter 96, with Trajan's reply
keyWorks.about: his trials of Christians, their worship before dawn, and Trajan's ruling that they were not to be sought out

remembered: Tertullian of Carthage, defending the Christians, attacked Trajan's reply to him: "It forbids them to be sought after as innocent, and it commands them to be punished as guilty."
Eusebius of Caesarea, working from Tertullian, calls him "one of the most noted of governors" and says the persecution "was to a certain degree checked" after Trajan's reply.
John Rolfe, who translated Suetonius, says Suetonius's life is known largely from Pliny's letters, and that Pliny got him a military post.

uncertain: Pliny writes as the official who held the trials. What he reports of the Christians' worship, he says, came from those who had left the faith.

The Library holds no edition of Pliny. The full English of the letter and of Trajan's reply is in Arthur McGiffert's note to Eusebius. Tertullian and Eusebius give only a short summary, without the deaconesses, the torture or the temples.
McGiffert dates his governorship to 110 or 111. Adolf Harnack dates the letter about 111 to 113.
No held primary source gives the years of his birth or death.
